title: The Litany of the Saints
hookLine: a long chant of names, sung at baptisms and ordinations: pray for us

lines: MEN LYING FACE DOWN ON STONE.
cards: A cathedral, full. At the front, a row of men in white lie face down on the stone floor, arms at their sides, not moving. They're about to be ordained priests.
Above them, a cantor begins to sing names. Holy Mary. Saint Michael.
Saint Peter, Saint Paul. After each name the whole church sings back the same short answer. Name, answer.
Name, answer. It goes on long enough that you stop counting and start listening.

teach.h: A LEADER CALLS; THE PEOPLE ANSWER.
teach.b: A litany is a prayer built from repetition: a leader calls out one line after another, and the people answer each time with the same response.
The Litany of the Saints is the one the Church sings at some of its biggest moments: at the Easter Vigil before new Christians are baptized, and at ordinations while the candidates lie on the floor.
It begins by asking the Lord for mercy.

Then the names: Mary first, then angels, John the Baptist and Joseph, apostles, martyrs, bishops and teachers, monks and nuns, and at last all the holy men and women. After each name the answer is pray for us.

It's an old request. Near the close of his first letter to the Thessalonians, Paul asks for it plainly, in the Douay-Rheims: "Brethren, pray for us." The litany turns that request toward the saints in heaven.
Parishes may add their own patrons, and the local saints of that place. Then the litany turns again: it asks God directly to deliver his people, and to hear their prayer.

teach.h: THE WHOLE WEEK IN ONE BREATH.
teach.b: Look back at this week. The saints of now: they're still here. The martyrology, someone on every day.
Beatification, the long line. Relics, bodies that loved God. Patrons, friends for the job.
The litany gathers all of it into one long breath: every name a life, tested and remembered, and a church full of people asking each of them for one thing.

how: The Litany of the Saints is sung at the Easter Vigil before baptisms and at ordinations while the candidates lie prostrate; a cantor sings each name and the congregation answers "pray for us".

o: a prayer of many lines with one repeated answer
a hymn sung only at a saint's funeral
a long list of sins read before confession

games.q: the week's words — tap the pairs.

s: the Litany of the Saints is sung at ordinations
the candidates lie face down while the church sings the names over them.
the litany only asks the saints and never prays to God directly

games.q: you're a candidate for ordination, lying on the cathedral floor. the cantor starts singing names. what does the church answer after each one?
games.why: pray for us, again and again: the same request Paul makes to the Thessalonians, turned toward the saints.

practice: Pick five names, Mary perhaps and four others you've met on this climb or already love, and say the first one slowly, in your head or out loud.

If you pray, follow it with the litany's answer, pray for us; if you don't, follow it with one full breath. Then the next name, and when you reach five, start again, slower: name and answer, name and breath.

wordCard.voice: Litany. A prayer of many lines with one repeated answer; the Litany of the Saints calls the names of the saints and answers, pray for us.

orig.note: Latin: pray for us, the answer sung after each name in the Litany of the Saints.

carryVoice: Your line: pray for us. An old request, sung by a whole church. See you tomorrow.
